headline: India's harvest miracle is draining its wells
dek: Norman Borlaug's short wheat gave India a record harvest in 1968.

slides.label: The bright idea
slides.title: Grow more on the same land
slides.text: Around 1960, West Pakistan grew about a ton of wheat per hectare and fell short of its needs every year. Feeding the wheat more fertilizer was no answer: past a point, the tall plants snapped.
slides.alt: A wheat field with a wide patch of tall stalks knocked flat to the ground
slides.credit: Wheat flattened by rain and wind, 2013. Azizkhan327. CC BY-SA 3.0.

slides.label: It worked
slides.title: Short wheat, big harvests
slides.text: Borlaug's team in Mexico bred dwarf wheat that could take two or three times the fertilizer and lifted top yields by more than 70 percent. Mexico grew all its own wheat by 1956. Pakistan and India took up the seed in the 1960s.
slides.alt: A broad field of ripe golden wheat beside a stretch of water under a cloudy sky in Punjab
slides.credit: Ripe wheat in Punjab, 2019. Harvinder Chandigarh. CC BY-SA 4.0.

slides.label: Wait, what?
slides.title: Rumors, then a stamp
slides.text: In Pakistan, the new seed first had to get past rumors that it would cause sterility. In India, the 1968 harvest was the biggest in the country's history and got its own postage stamp: "The Indian Wheat Revolution 1968."

slides.label: The backfire
slides.title: Wells that keep getting deeper
slides.statLabel: of groundwater lost in three northwest Indian states, 2002 to 2008, likely from irrigation and other human use
slides.text: The new seeds paid off when fed water and fertilizer. Punjab moved to nearly 80 percent rice and wheat, two thirsty crops, watered from wells. Farmers who once pumped from 5 to 10 feet down now drill 200 to 300 feet.
also: Source: Rodell, Velicogna and Famiglietti, Nature, 2009
slides.alt: A pump engine and pipe at a brick tube well beside a green wheat field
slides.credit: Tube well in Mansa district, Punjab, India, 2012. Tari Buttar. CC0.

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: Partly
slides.text: In 1970 Borlaug called the Green Revolution "a temporary success" that bought "a breathing space," though his worry was population, not water. Punjab's water table was falling 18 cm a year by the mid-1980s, and about a meter a year by 2010.

slides.label: The ledger
slides.title: Worth it?
gains: Cereal harvests in the developing world tripled in 50 years, on 30 percent more land (PNAS, 2012)
India's record wheat crop of 17 million tons in 1968 (Nobel Committee)
Mexico self-supporting in wheat by 1956 (Nobel Committee)
costs: 109 cubic kilometers of groundwater lost in northwest India, 2002 to 2008 (Nature, 2009)
Punjab pumping 45 percent more groundwater each year than rain puts back (Columbia Water Center, 2010)
Water use, soil damage and chemical runoff beyond the fields (PNAS, 2012)
slides.text: The harvests ended chronic food shortages across much of the developing world and spared land from the plow. The water bill is still arriving. You decide if it was worth it.

slides.label: Credit for trying
slides.title: We owe him one
slides.text: Borlaug took on hunger at the scale of whole nations, and the harvests came. A later review found the damage came less from the seeds than from policies that made water and fertilizer cheap to overuse. Fixing that is still unfinished work.

slides.label: How the pattern works
slides.title: Water that felt free
slides.text: Punjab charged farmers a flat fee for the electricity that runs their pumps, so pumping more cost nothing extra. Guaranteed prices kept rice and wheat in the ground. The harvest pays every season. The aquifer bill comes due over decades.

slides.label: How you do this
slides.title: Ship now, fix later
slides.text: A team hits every deadline by skipping tests and notes. For a year, output looks great. Then every change breaks something, and new features take twice as long. The speed was borrowed, and the loan came due.
also: Putting off a roof repair until the ceiling stains
Skipping sleep to finish one big week

slides.label: Lessons
slides.title: What we take from it
items: A harvest shows up every season. A falling water table shows up slowly, a meter at a time.
When a resource costs a flat fee, nobody has a reason to use less of it.
The people who make a tool and the people who set the prices around it share the outcome.
